leitner_plan.new: Earthquake case studies and tropical storms (7)

cards.title: Natural hazards and hazard risk
cards.question: What is a natural hazard, and what affects the level of risk?
points: A natural hazard is a natural process that could cause death, injury or damage to property.
Tectonic (geological) hazards: earthquakes, volcanoes. Atmospheric (meteorological) hazards: tropical storms, droughts, extreme weather.
Hazard risk is the chance of being affected. It rises with population density, poverty and lack of preparation.
Other factors: urbanisation, farming on fertile volcanic soils, and climate change making some hazards more frequent.
cards.watch_out: A hazard only becomes a disaster when it affects people. An earthquake in an empty desert is a hazard, not a disaster.
cards.grade9: Explain why the same magnitude hazard can cause very different deaths in an HIC and an LIC, using vulnerability and capacity to respond.

cards.title: Plate tectonics and the structure of the Earth
cards.question: Why do tectonic plates move, and where are earthquakes and volcanoes found?
points: The Earth has a crust, mantle, outer core and inner core. The crust is broken into tectonic plates.
Oceanic crust is thinner and denser; continental crust is thicker and less dense.
Plates move because of convection currents in the mantle, and slab pull at subduction zones.
Most earthquakes and volcanoes are found in narrow belts along plate margins, such as the Pacific Ring of Fire.
cards.watch_out: Some volcanoes, such as Hawaii, form away from margins over hot spots. Say most, not all.
cards.grade9: Use evidence from a map: describe the pattern with named places and direction, not just near plate boundaries.

cards.title: Destructive plate margins
cards.question: What happens at a destructive plate margin?
points: An oceanic plate and a continental plate move towards each other.
The denser oceanic plate is forced down (subducted) beneath the continental plate.
Friction causes strong earthquakes. The oceanic plate melts in the mantle, and magma rises to form explosive composite volcanoes.
Example: the Nazca plate subducting under the South American plate, forming the Andes and causing the Chile 2010 earthquake.
cards.watch_out: Destructive margins have both earthquakes and volcanoes; conservative margins have earthquakes only.
cards.grade9: Use the term subduction zone and explain why the volcanoes are explosive: thick, gas rich magma.

cards.title: Constructive and conservative margins
cards.question: What happens at constructive and conservative plate margins?
points: Constructive: plates move apart. Magma rises to fill the gap, forming new crust and gentle shield volcanoes. Example: the Mid Atlantic Ridge and Iceland.
Earthquakes at constructive margins are usually small.
Conservative: plates slide past each other in the same or opposite directions. Pressure builds then releases as earthquakes. No volcanoes.
Example: the San Andreas Fault in California, where the Pacific and North American plates meet.
cards.watch_out: At a conservative margin no crust is made or destroyed, so there is no magma and no volcanoes.
cards.hook: Constructive constructs crust; conservative conserves it.
cards.grade9: Explain why shield volcanoes are gentle: runny, low gas basalt lava flows easily.

cards.title: Why people live in hazard zones
cards.question: Why do people continue to live in areas at risk from tectonic hazards?
points: Volcanic soils are very fertile, which is good for farming.
Geothermal energy and tourism create jobs and income (for example Iceland).
Minerals and precious metals are found near volcanoes.
People may be poor, unable to move, have family ties, or believe the risk is low because events are rare.
cards.watch_out: Do not only list positives. Examiners also reward reasons linked to choice, such as poverty and lack of awareness.
cards.grade9: Weigh benefits against risk and say that better monitoring makes living there safer in HICs.

cards.title: Chile 2010 (HIC or NEE example)
cards.question: What were the effects of and responses to the Chile earthquake in 2010?
points: 27 February 2010, magnitude 8.8, off the coast of central Chile at a destructive margin.
Primary effects: about 500 deaths, hundreds of thousands of homes damaged, roads, bridges and ports damaged.
Secondary effects: a tsunami hit coastal towns; fires; power and water cut off for days.
Responses: emergency services acted quickly, roads were repaired fast, and the government planned housing reconstruction. Strict building codes kept deaths low.
cards.watch_out: Learn the difference: primary effects are caused directly by the shaking; secondary effects happen later as a result, such as the tsunami.
cards.hook: Chile: big quake, small death toll, because it was prepared.
cards.grade9: Compare with Nepal using numbers to show how level of development changes the effects.

cards.title: Nepal 2015 (LIC example)
cards.question: What were the effects of and responses to the Nepal earthquake in 2015?
points: 25 April 2015, magnitude 7.8, epicentre about 80 km northwest of Kathmandu, where the Indian plate pushes into the Eurasian plate.
Primary effects: about 9000 deaths, around 3 million people made homeless, historic buildings destroyed.
Secondary effects: avalanches on Mount Everest, landslides blocked roads and rivers, loss of tourism income.
Responses: international aid, search and rescue teams from abroad, field hospitals. Rebuilding was slow because of poor roads and funding.
cards.watch_out: Nepal's earthquake was smaller than Chile's but killed far more people. Do not assume bigger magnitude means more deaths.
cards.grade9: Explain the reasons: poorly built homes, remote mountain villages, and limited money for rescue.

cards.title: Reducing the risk: the four Ps
cards.question: How can monitoring, prediction, protection and planning reduce the risk from tectonic hazards?
points: Monitoring: seismometers, tiltmeters and gas sensors detect warning signs, especially for volcanoes.
Prediction: earthquakes cannot be accurately predicted; volcanic eruptions can sometimes be predicted from monitoring.
Protection: earthquake resistant buildings with cross bracing, rubber shock absorbers and flexible frames.
Planning: hazard maps, evacuation routes, emergency kits and earthquake drills.
cards.watch_out: Do not write that scientists can predict exactly when an earthquake will happen. They cannot.
cards.hook: The four Ps: Monitor, Predict, Protect, Plan.
cards.grade9: Evaluate which P is most effective in an LIC: planning and education are cheapest and save many lives.

cards.title: Global atmospheric circulation
cards.question: How does global atmospheric circulation create areas of high and low pressure?
points: The sun heats the equator most. Warm air rises, creating low pressure and heavy rain (tropical rainforests).
Air spreads out, cools and sinks at about 30° north and south, creating high pressure and dry conditions (hot deserts).
Three cells in each hemisphere: the Hadley, Ferrel and Polar cells.
Winds blow from high to low pressure at the surface, curved by the Earth's rotation.
cards.watch_out: Rising air means low pressure and rain. Sinking air means high pressure and dry weather.
cards.hook: Rise, rain, low. Sink, sun, high.
cards.grade9: Link circulation to both topics: it explains where tropical storms form and why hot deserts are at 30°.

cards.title: Tropical storms: formation and structure
cards.question: Where and how do tropical storms form, and what is their structure?
points: They form over oceans of at least 27 °C, between 5° and 30° north and south of the equator.
Warm, moist air rises quickly, creating low pressure. Water vapour condenses, releasing heat that powers the storm.
The Coriolis effect, from the Earth's spin, makes the storm rotate. It moves with the prevailing winds and weakens over land or cooler water.
Structure: a calm eye of sinking air, surrounded by the eyewall with the strongest winds and heaviest rain.
cards.watch_out: Tropical storms do not form right on the equator because the Coriolis effect there is too weak to make them spin.
cards.hook: 27 degrees, 5 to 30 degrees: warm water and the right latitude.
cards.grade9: Explain why storms weaken over land: they lose their supply of warm, moist air.

cards.title: Typhoon Haiyan 2013
cards.question: What were the effects of and responses to Typhoon Haiyan in the Philippines?
points: November 2013, one of the strongest tropical storms recorded, with winds over 300 km/h.
Primary effects: about 6300 deaths, a storm surge of about 5 m in Tacloban, homes and buildings flattened.
Secondary effects: around 4 million people displaced, shortages of food, water and shelter, disease, loss of farming and fishing jobs.
Responses: evacuation of around 800 000 people beforehand, international aid, emergency shelters, later rebuilding with storm surge warnings.
cards.watch_out: The storm surge caused most deaths, not only the wind. Mention it in effects answers.
cards.grade9: Evaluate the response: warnings existed, but many people did not understand what a storm surge was.

cards.title: Reducing the effects of tropical storms and climate change
cards.question: How can the effects of tropical storms be reduced, and how might climate change affect them?
points: Monitoring and prediction with satellites and aircraft gives several days' warning of the track.
Protection: storm shelters, sea walls, buildings on stilts, reinforced roofs.
Planning: evacuation routes, education and emergency supplies.
Climate change may make storms more intense, and warmer seas may let them form further from the equator.
cards.watch_out: Scientists are less sure that storms will become more frequent. Say more intense, not definitely more frequent.
cards.grade9: Use may and could when writing about climate change effects; certainty claims lose credibility.

cards.title: UK weather hazards
cards.question: What weather hazards affect the UK, and is UK weather becoming more extreme?
points: Hazards: river and coastal flooding, storms and strong winds, heatwaves, droughts, snow and ice.
Evidence of more extreme weather: record temperatures (over 40 °C in July 2022), more frequent heavy rain events, wetter winters.
Several of the warmest years on record in the UK have been since 2000.
Extreme weather affects transport, health, farming and homes.
cards.watch_out: One extreme event does not prove a trend. Use a pattern of records over many years as evidence.
cards.grade9: Balance your answer: records are short, and some years are not extreme, so the evidence suggests rather than proves.

cards.title: Somerset Levels floods 2014
cards.question: What caused the Somerset Levels floods, and what were the effects and responses?
points: Causes: very high rainfall in January and February 2014, high tides, and rivers (the Parrett and the Tone) that had not been dredged.
Social effects: about 600 homes flooded, villages such as Muchelney cut off, power cuts.
Economic effects: large areas of farmland under water for weeks, livestock moved, roads and the railway closed.
Responses: emergency rescue, then a 20 year Flood Action Plan costing around £100 million, including dredging about 8 km of river and raising roads.
cards.watch_out: Low lying, flat land is a physical cause; lack of dredging is a human cause. Name both.
cards.grade9: Classify effects as social, economic and environmental, and responses as immediate and long term.

cards.title: Evidence for climate change
cards.question: What is the evidence that the climate has changed since the beginning of the Quaternary period?
points: The Quaternary period is roughly the last 2.6 million years, with glacial and interglacial periods.
Ice cores: air bubbles show past carbon dioxide levels and temperatures.
Tree rings, pollen and historical records such as paintings and diaries.
Recent evidence: rising global temperatures, shrinking glaciers and Arctic sea ice, and rising sea levels.
cards.watch_out: Ice cores and tree rings give evidence for different time spans. Ice cores go back hundreds of thousands of years; tree rings a few thousand.
cards.hook: ICE TREES: ice cores and tree rings are the two big pieces of evidence.
cards.grade9: Explain how reliable each source is; for example, historical records are local and may be biased.

cards.title: Causes and management of climate change
cards.question: What are the natural and human causes of climate change, and how can it be managed?
points: Natural causes: changes in the Earth's orbit (Milankovitch cycles), changes in solar output, and volcanic eruptions.
Human causes: burning fossil fuels, farming (methane from cattle and rice), and deforestation, which increase the enhanced greenhouse effect.
Mitigation (reducing causes): renewable energy, carbon capture, planting trees, international agreements.
Adaptation (living with effects): flood defences, drought resistant crops, managing water supplies.
cards.watch_out: Mitigation tackles the causes; adaptation copes with the effects. These are often confused.
cards.hook: Mitigate the cause, adapt to the effect.
cards.grade9: Evaluate: mitigation needs global cooperation, but adaptation can be done locally and quickly.

cards.title: Ecosystems and food webs
cards.question: What are the parts of an ecosystem, and how are they linked?
points: An ecosystem is a community of plants and animals interacting with each other and their environment (biotic and abiotic parts).
Producers make energy from sunlight. Consumers eat other organisms. Decomposers break down dead material.
Food chains and food webs show how energy passes between organisms.
Nutrient cycling: nutrients move between the soil, plants (biomass) and leaf litter.
cards.watch_out: A change to one part of a food web affects the others. Explain the knock on effect, not only the first change.
cards.grade9: Use a named small scale UK ecosystem, such as a pond, to explain interdependence.

cards.title: Characteristics of hot deserts
cards.question: What are the climate, soil and location of hot deserts?
points: Found around 30° north and south of the equator, where high pressure air sinks, such as the Sahara and the Thar.
Low rainfall: under 250 mm per year, and it is unreliable.
Very hot days (often over 40 °C) but cold nights, because clear skies let heat escape.
Soils are thin, sandy or stony, and low in nutrients, because there is little plant matter.
cards.watch_out: Deserts are defined by low rainfall, not heat. Some deserts are cold.
cards.hook: 250 mm a year: the desert line.
cards.grade9: Explain the large daily temperature range using the lack of cloud cover.

cards.title: Adaptations and interdependence
cards.question: How have plants and animals adapted to hot desert conditions?
points: Cacti: thick, waxy skin to reduce water loss; spines instead of leaves; shallow, wide roots to collect rain quickly; stems that store water.
Some plants have very long tap roots to reach deep groundwater.
Camels: humps store fat, wide feet for sand, long eyelashes and closable nostrils against sand, can drink large amounts quickly.
Many animals are nocturnal to avoid the heat.
cards.watch_out: A camel's hump stores fat, not water. This is a common wrong answer.
cards.grade9: Link adaptations to interdependence: plants provide food and shade, animals spread seeds.

cards.title: Biodiversity in hot deserts
cards.question: What are the issues related to biodiversity in hot deserts?
points: Biodiversity is low compared to rainforests because of the harsh climate.
Species are often endemic (found only there) and specially adapted.
Threats: overgrazing, climate change, hunting, and development such as mining and tourism.
Loss of one species can break food webs because there are few species to replace it.
cards.watch_out: Low biodiversity does not mean deserts are unimportant. Their species are rare and easily lost.
cards.grade9: Explain why low biodiversity makes desert ecosystems fragile.

cards.title: Thar Desert: development opportunities
cards.question: What development opportunities does the Thar Desert offer?
points: Location: northwest India and Pakistan, mainly in Rajasthan.
Mineral extraction: gypsum, feldspar, limestone and other minerals; an oil field at Barmer.
Energy: large solar and wind farms, such as the Jaisalmer wind park, because of strong sun and wind.
Farming with irrigation from the Indira Gandhi Canal; tourism such as camel safaris and the desert festival in Jaisalmer.
cards.watch_out: Name the specific places (Barmer, Jaisalmer, Indira Gandhi Canal). Case study answers without detail stay in the lower levels.
cards.grade9: Evaluate which opportunity brings the most benefit to local people rather than to companies.

cards.title: Thar Desert: development challenges
cards.question: What challenges does development face in the Thar Desert?
points: Extreme temperatures, sometimes near 50 °C in summer, make working outdoors difficult.
Water supply: low rainfall and high evaporation; groundwater can be salty, and the canal loses water to evaporation.
Inaccessibility: few roads, and sand blows over them; long distances make services expensive.
Over use of land and water can cause desertification.
cards.watch_out: Challenges must be linked to the desert environment, not general problems like crime.
cards.grade9: Show how the canal is both an opportunity and a challenge: it allows farming but causes salinisation and waterlogging.

cards.title: Desertification: causes
cards.question: What is desertification and what causes it?
points: Desertification is the process by which land becomes drier and degraded, until it is like a desert.
Climate change: less rainfall and higher temperatures.
Population growth leads to over grazing, over cultivation and removal of fuel wood, leaving soil exposed.
Over abstraction of water lowers water tables. Soil erosion by wind and rain then removes fertile topsoil.
cards.watch_out: Desertification happens at the edges of deserts, such as the Sahel, not inside the desert itself.
cards.hook: Grazing, growing, gathering wood, guzzling water: the four human Gs.
cards.grade9: Show the cycle: removing plants exposes soil, soil is eroded, fewer plants can grow, so the land degrades further.

cards.title: Desertification: reducing the risk
cards.question: What strategies can reduce the risk of desertification?
points: Water and soil management: drip irrigation, rainwater harvesting.
Tree planting: trees bind the soil, give shade and act as windbreaks. The Great Green Wall across Africa is an example.
Appropriate technology: stone lines (magic stones) slow runoff so water soaks into the soil; solar cookers reduce the need for fuel wood.
Educating farmers to rotate grazing and crops.
cards.watch_out: Appropriate technology must suit local people: cheap, simple and easy to maintain.
cards.grade9: Evaluate strategies by cost, scale and sustainability. Stone lines are cheap and local; the Great Green Wall is huge but slow.

cards.title: Case study facts to learn
cards.question: Can you recall the key facts for each case study?
points: Chile 2010: magnitude 8.8, about 500 deaths, tsunami, quick recovery.
Nepal 2015: magnitude 7.8, about 9000 deaths, 3 million homeless, avalanches, international aid.
Haiyan 2013: Philippines, about 6300 deaths, 5 m storm surge, about 4 million displaced.
Somerset Levels 2014: about 600 homes flooded, £100 million action plan, 8 km of dredging.
Thar Desert: Barmer oil, Jaisalmer wind and tourism, Indira Gandhi Canal.
cards.watch_out: Learn three facts per case study: a number, a place and a response.

written.q: Explain what happens at a destructive plate margin.
model: Oceanic and continental plates move towards each other (1)
The denser oceanic plate is subducted (1)
Friction causes earthquakes (1)
The plate melts, and rising magma forms explosive volcanoes (1)

written.q: Compare the effects of a tectonic hazard in two areas of contrasting wealth.
model: Named HIC or NEE example with magnitude, such as Chile 2010, 8.8 (1)
Named LIC example, such as Nepal 2015, 7.8 (1)
Comparison of deaths: about 500 compared with about 9000 (1)
Comparison of secondary effects: tsunami compared with avalanches and landslides (1)
Reason linked to development, such as building codes (1)
Comparative language throughout, such as whereas or in contrast (1)
Ocean temperature of at least 27 °C (1)
Between 5° and 30° from the equator (1)
Warm moist air rises rapidly, creating low pressure (1)
Condensation releases heat, powering the storm (1)
Coriolis effect causes rotation (1)
Cool air sinks in the centre, forming the eye (1)

written.q: Assess the extent to which the effects of an extreme weather event in the UK were caused by human activity. Use a named example.
model: Named example, such as the Somerset Levels floods 2014 (1)
Physical causes: very high rainfall and high tides (2)
Physical cause: flat, low lying land (1)
Human cause: rivers not dredged, reducing capacity (2)
Effects described with facts, such as about 600 homes flooded (1)
Judgement on the relative importance of physical and human causes (2)

written.q: To what extent does a hot desert environment provide more opportunities than challenges for development? Use a named example.
model: Named example, the Thar Desert (1)
Opportunities: Barmer oil and minerals (1)
Opportunities: solar and wind energy, Jaisalmer (1)
Opportunities: farming with the Indira Gandhi Canal, tourism (1)
Challenges: extreme temperatures (1)
Challenges: water supply and evaporation (1)
Challenges: inaccessibility (1)
Justified overall judgement (2)

written.q: Explain how human activity can cause desertification.
model: Over grazing removes vegetation (1)
Removing fuel wood exposes the soil (1)
Over cultivation exhausts the soil (1)
Exposed soil is eroded by wind and rain, leading to degradation (1)

exam_tips.timing: Written exam about 50 minutes. Spend roughly a minute per mark, and save 12 minutes for a 9 mark question.
section_a: For describe questions, say what you see. For explain questions, give reasons with because.
Read graphs and maps carefully and quote numbers with units.
section_b: 6 and 9 mark answers need developed points (point, explain, link).
9 mark assess or to what extent questions need a clear judgement.
Use geographical terms such as subduction, Coriolis effect and desertification.
grade9: Explain processes as a linked chain, not a list of features. The oceanic plate sinks and melts, then magma rises.
Judge with evidence and a limitation. Prediction saves lives, but a storm path can still change.
Use place detail only when it answers the question asked.
Compare HIC and LIC case studies using numbers and reasons linked to development.
Make your judgement early and return to it in the conclusion.

mcq.q: What is a natural hazard?
mcq.a: A natural process that could cause death, injury or damage
w: A natural event in an uninhabited area
mcq.e: It becomes a hazard because it threatens people.

mcq.q: Which is an atmospheric hazard?
mcq.e: Atmospheric hazards are caused by weather.

mcq.q: Which type of crust is denser?
w: It depends on its age only
mcq.e: Denser oceanic crust is subducted.

mcq.q: What drives plate movement?
mcq.a: Convection currents in the mantle and slab pull
mcq.e: Heat from the core drives mantle convection.

mcq.q: What happens at a destructive margin?
mcq.a: Oceanic crust is subducted under continental crust
mcq.e: Subduction causes earthquakes and explosive volcanoes.

mcq.q: Which margin has earthquakes but no volcanoes?
mcq.e: No magma is produced when plates slide past.

mcq.q: Which is an example of a constructive margin?
mcq.e: Plates move apart and new crust forms.

mcq.q: Which type of volcano forms at constructive margins?
mcq.e: Runny basalt lava forms gentle slopes.

mcq.q: Which is a reason people live near volcanoes?
mcq.e: Volcanic ash breaks down into fertile soil.

mcq.q: Which increases hazard risk?
mcq.e: More people means more exposure.

mcq.q: What magnitude was the Chile earthquake of 2010?
mcq.e: It was one of the largest earthquakes ever recorded.

mcq.q: Roughly how many people died in the Nepal earthquake of 2015?
mcq.e: Far more than Chile, despite a smaller magnitude.

mcq.q: Which was a secondary effect of the Chile earthquake?
mcq.e: Secondary effects follow from the primary effects.

mcq.q: Which was a secondary effect of the Nepal earthquake?
mcq.e: Shaking triggered avalanches and landslides.

mcq.q: Why did fewer people die in Chile than in Nepal?
mcq.a: Chile had stricter building codes and better emergency services
mcq.e: Level of development affects vulnerability.

mcq.q: Which of the four Ps uses seismometers?
mcq.e: Seismometers detect ground movement.

mcq.q: Which is an example of protection?
mcq.e: Protection means making structures safer.

mcq.q: Can scientists accurately predict when an earthquake will happen?
mcq.e: Volcanoes can sometimes be predicted; earthquakes cannot.

mcq.q: What sea temperature is needed for a tropical storm to form?
mcq.e: Warm water supplies the energy.

mcq.q: Between which latitudes do tropical storms usually form?
mcq.e: Too close to the equator, there is not enough Coriolis effect.

mcq.q: What makes a tropical storm spin?
mcq.e: The Earth's rotation deflects the winds.

mcq.q: What is the eye of a tropical storm?
mcq.a: A calm area of sinking air in the centre
w: The area with the strongest winds
The front edge of the storm
mcq.e: The strongest winds are in the eyewall around it.

mcq.q: What pressure is found where air rises at the equator?
mcq.e: Rising air creates low pressure and rain.

mcq.q: Which cell lies between the equator and 30°?
mcq.e: Hadley, Ferrel, Polar from equator to pole.

mcq.q: Which country was hit by Typhoon Haiyan in 2013?
mcq.e: It devastated Tacloban.

mcq.q: What caused many of the deaths in Typhoon Haiyan?
mcq.a: A storm surge of about 5 m
mcq.e: Sea water flooded coastal areas.

mcq.q: How might climate change affect tropical storms?
w: They will only form on land
mcq.e: Warmer seas give more energy.

mcq.q: Which rivers flooded on the Somerset Levels in 2014?
mcq.e: Lack of dredging made flooding worse.

mcq.q: Roughly how many homes were flooded on the Somerset Levels in 2014?
mcq.e: Villages such as Muchelney were cut off.

mcq.q: What was the cost of the Somerset Levels Flood Action Plan?
mcq.e: It included 8 km of dredging.

mcq.q: What does ice core evidence show?
mcq.a: Past carbon dioxide levels and temperatures
mcq.e: Air bubbles trap ancient atmosphere.

mcq.q: Which is a natural cause of climate change?
mcq.e: Milankovitch cycles.

mcq.q: What is mitigation?
mcq.a: Reducing the causes of climate change
mcq.e: Adaptation is coping with effects.

mcq.q: Which is an example of adaptation?
mcq.e: Adaptation responds to the effects.

mcq.q: What is a producer?
mcq.a: An organism that makes energy from sunlight
w: An organism that breaks down dead material
mcq.e: Plants are producers.

mcq.q: What do decomposers do?
mcq.a: Break down dead material and return nutrients to the soil
mcq.e: Bacteria and fungi are decomposers.

mcq.q: What is the maximum yearly rainfall of a hot desert?
mcq.e: Deserts are defined by low rainfall.

mcq.q: Why are desert nights cold?
w: The sun is weaker in deserts
Winds bring cold air from the poles
mcq.e: No cloud cover means heat is lost quickly.

mcq.q: What does a camel's hump store?
mcq.e: The fat can be broken down for energy.

mcq.q: Why do cacti have spines instead of leaves?
mcq.a: To reduce water loss and deter animals
mcq.e: Smaller surface area means less transpiration.

mcq.q: Why do some desert plants have long tap roots?
mcq.e: Water may be far below the surface.

mcq.q: Why is biodiversity low in hot deserts?
mcq.a: The extreme climate limits which species can survive
mcq.e: Few species are adapted to the harsh conditions.

mcq.q: Where is the Thar Desert?
mcq.e: Mainly in Rajasthan.

mcq.q: What brings irrigation water to the Thar Desert?
mcq.e: It allows crops to be grown.

mcq.q: Where in the Thar Desert is oil extracted?
mcq.e: Barmer has a major oil field.

mcq.q: Which is a challenge of developing the Thar Desert?
mcq.e: Summer temperatures can approach 50 °C.

mcq.q: What is desertification?
mcq.a: Land becoming drier and degraded until it is like a desert
w: The movement of a desert towards the sea
mcq.e: It happens at desert edges.

mcq.q: Which is a human cause of desertification?
mcq.e: Animals remove the plants that protect the soil.

mcq.q: How do stone lines (magic stones) help?
mcq.a: They slow runoff so water soaks into the soil
mcq.e: A cheap appropriate technology.

mcq.q: What is the Great Green Wall?
mcq.a: A belt of trees planted across Africa to stop desertification
w: A wall to keep sand out of cities
mcq.e: Trees bind soil and act as windbreaks.

vocab.meaning: How likely people are to be harmed by a hazard
vocab.example: Poor housing increases vulnerability to earthquakes.

vocab.meaning: When one plate is forced down beneath another
vocab.example: Subduction of the Nazca plate causes earthquakes in Chile.

vocab.meaning: The size or strength of an earthquake
vocab.example: The Chile earthquake had a magnitude of 8.8.

vocab.meaning: Action to reduce the causes or severity of something
vocab.example: Renewable energy is a form of climate change mitigation.

vocab.meaning: A change that helps a species or people cope with conditions
vocab.example: Long roots are an adaptation to desert life.

vocab.meaning: The process of land becoming desert like
vocab.example: Desertification is a serious problem in the Sahel.

vocab.meaning: The variety of living things in an area
When parts of an ecosystem rely on each other
vocab.example: Interdependence means losing one species affects others.
Early evacuation saved many lives before Typhoon Haiyan.

vocab.meaning: Basic structures such as roads, power and water supply
vocab.example: The earthquake destroyed infrastructure such as bridges and roads.
